clue.text: Could I fib with Ofgas? No d___ problem! I'm an imposter!

indicators.note: a problem is a muddle, so the gathered letters are in disorder and must be sorted out
the gap after the letter shows that one letter is to be refused, struck out of the neighbouring word

parts.note: taken as written, before its D is dropped
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written; Ofgas was the British gas industry regulator

explanation.surface: A conman posing as a gas-regulator official breezily admits he could lie, then confesses to being an imposter.
explanation.walkthrough: COULD loses its D, then COUL plus I FIB OFGAS are rearranged to give BOGUS OFFICIAL. Ofgas, the old regulator, makes a fake official from it a plausible character.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone falsely posing as a person in authority, such as a meter inspector, is a classic doorstep fraudster.

clue.text: Warning! Half of my shares go into her personal cover

indicators.note: things that go into something end up inside it, so these letters sit within the warning word

parts.note: a boding is a foreboding or omen, a warning

indicators.note: a two-letter word cut in half keeps just one of its letters, here the second

parts.note: the back half of the two-letter word
stock is a holding of shares

explanation.surface: An investor sounds an alarm as half their shares disappear into a woman's private cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warning' looks like an exclamation but is a noun for an omen, opened up to take the other letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A body stocking is a skin-tight one-piece garment covering a woman's torso and often limbs.

clue.text: Compete in Lac Leman, on dit, with that 1904 Darracq

indicators.note: the competing word is set in the middle of the French place name

parts.note: Lac Leman is Lake Geneva, and the French ('on dit', as they say) call the city Geneve
to vie is to compete

explanation.surface: A veteran French car is competing in a race by Lake Geneva, so they say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On dit' is French for 'they say', telling you to give the city's name the French way, without the final A.
explanation.definitionFit: Genevieve was the 1904 Darracq motor car starring in the 1953 British comedy film about the London to Brighton veteran car run.

clue.text: Spiritless horse full of beans? Singularly, quite the reverse!

indicators.note: 'quite the reverse' swaps the roles, so the bean is the one that is filled and the horse goes inside it

parts.note: taken singularly, one soy bean
gee-gee, a child's word for a horse
instruction, not letters: make the beans singular and swap which one holds the other

explanation.surface: A listless horse described as full of beans, which is the opposite of lively.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's horse full of beans is swapped round: one bean holds the horse. 'Full of beans' means lively, the opposite of the definition, which is part of the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Soggy can mean dull and lacking vitality, as a soggy performance has no energy or spirit.

clue.text: See 1
Are wet otherwise, donning our gear

indicators.note: a word donning something puts it on, wrapping round it like clothes

parts.note: taken as written; it is the wrapper

indicators.note: otherwise means in another way, so these two words are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Hikers would be soaked otherwise, so they put on their waterproofs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our gear' reads as a phrase, but 'our' is the wrapper and 'gear' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Outerwear is clothing worn over other clothes, such as coats and jackets, which counts as gear.

clue.text: Force that it following land one had to fight for

definitions.text: land one had to fight for

parts.note: F is the physics symbol for force
read as 'that is', i.e., abbreviated IE
f. is the abbreviation for following, as in page references

explanation.surface: A historical note about some territory that had to be fought for.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'that it' appears to be a slip for 'that is', which gives i.e.
explanation.definitionFit: A fief was an estate granted by a feudal lord in return for military service by the holder.

clue.text: Author with stake in church bibles

parts.note: Church of England

indicators.note: the stake is put in among the letters for the holy books

parts.note: Revised Versions of the Bible, abbreviated RV
the stake put up in poker

explanation.surface: A writer who has a financial interest in a company printing church bibles.
explanation.walkthrough: RV, the Revised Version, is a standard crossword abbreviation for a bible; the plural takes an S.
explanation.definitionFit: Miguel de Cervantes was the Spanish writer of Don Quixote, so he is an example of an author.

clue.text: Grey's name in The Times

definitions.note: Grey's first name: the possessive leads into 'name'

indicators.note: the abbreviation sits in the middle of the long periods word

parts.note: ages are times or eras
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A newspaper mention of someone called Grey in The Times.
explanation.walkthrough: N goes inside AGES. Agnes Grey is the title heroine of Anne Brontë's first novel; 'name' serves both the definition and the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The governess heroine of Anne Brontë's novel is Agnes Grey, so that is her given, Christian name.

clue.text: Do understand! I'm not Unthorn!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a plea to be correctly understood
second meaning: the setter, Bunthorne, asking not to have his name garbled with letters lost

explanation.walkthrough: The setter's pseudonym is Bunthorne; Unthorn is that name with its first and last letters lopped off, a wrong version of him.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a common appeal against being misinterpreted, and literally asks that the speaker not be mistaken or misnamed.

clue.text: Congressional adviser, as this expert might be

indicators.note: what words might be is something other than they are now, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone advising members of the US Congress, as a specialist might.
explanation.walkthrough: Congress looks political, as in Washington, but here it means sexual intercourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Congress is an old word for sexual intercourse, so a counsellor who helps couples with it advises on congress.

clue.text: One supports G&S with second return of nest eggs

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the two following words are read backwards

parts.note: a drey or dray is a squirrel's nest
ova is Latin for eggs

explanation.surface: A backer of a G&S production gets a second return on their savings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nest eggs' looks like savings, but splits into nest and eggs. G&S is Gilbert and Sullivan, whose operas played at the Savoy Theatre in London.
explanation.definitionFit: A Savoyard is an enthusiast or performer of the Gilbert and Sullivan comic operas staged at the Savoy Theatre.

clue.text: Zoroastrian from average diocese

parts.note: par is the normal or average level
a see is a bishop's diocese

explanation.surface: A follower of Zoroaster who lives in an ordinary diocese.
explanation.definitionFit: Parsees are the Zoroastrian community of India, descended from Persians who fled religious persecution.

clue.text: Prevail on Dark Lady, would you say?

parts.note: surface reading: someone persuading the mysterious woman of Shakespeare's sonnets
setter's reading: to prevail over someone so completely as to swamp them, as Shakespeare's passion did

explanation.surface: Someone trying to persuade Shakespeare's Dark Lady, the mysterious woman of his sonnets.
explanation.walkthrough: The parse is uncertain: 'would you say' suggests a sound-alike for the Dark Lady, but no clear one appears; the whole reads as a cryptic hint at prevailing over her.
explanation.definitionFit: To overwhelm is to overpower or defeat completely, so it means prevailing over someone utterly.

clue.text: Wine lover becoming a wild glutton

indicators.note: becoming is turning into something else, so these letters change their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A wine enthusiast turns into a greedy brute.
explanation.definitionFit: The wolverine is a fierce wild animal of the weasel family, also known as the glutton for its voracious appetite.

clue.text: Mouldy attempt to rise in my 22

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the turned attempt sits inside the stomach complaint

parts.note: the answer to 22 down, the gripes

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading upwards, so the attempt word is turned back

parts.note: a go is an attempt

explanation.surface: A mouldy meal makes someone's stomach pains try to come back up.
explanation.walkthrough: The '22' is a cross-reference: the answer to 22 down is put in its place.
explanation.definitionFit: Mycologic means relating to the study of fungi, and moulds are fungi, so the setter stretches it to mouldy.

clue.text: One's cheerfully drunk when in drink

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a salute drunk in someone's honour
second meaning: browned bread, once floated in wine or ale

explanation.walkthrough: Spiced bread was once put in a cup of wine, which is how drinking a salute got its name.
explanation.definitionFit: A salute raised with glasses is drunk cheerfully, and the grilled bread was the thing once dunked in the cup.

clue.text: 'ang about! Attack the target!

parts.note: to hang about a place is to haunt it; the apostrophe drops the H, Cockney-style
a sally is a sudden attack by besieged troops

explanation.surface: A Cockney shout to wait, then an order to fire on the target.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aunt Sally is a traditional British fairground game in which players throw sticks at a wooden figure's head.
explanation.definitionFit: Figuratively, an Aunt Sally is a person or idea set up to be easily criticised, a target of attack.

clue.text: Royal Mistress heard in "The Ring"

indicators.note: heard means the mistress's name is listened to rather than spelt

parts.note: Nell Gwyn was the mistress of King Charles II

explanation.surface: A king's mistress appears at a performance of Wagner's The Ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The silent K means the sound of Nell matches the bell word exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: A knell is the solemn sound of a bell rung, especially for a death, so it is a ring.

clue.text: Can secure insecure dissent

indicators.note: something insecure is unsteady and loose, so the letters come apart and regroup

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A wobbly argument about whether a shaky disagreement can be locked down.
explanation.definitionFit: Recusance is refusal to submit to authority, historically Catholics refusing to attend Anglican services, hence dissent.

clue.text: Jack Frost's child?

parts.note: surface reading: the offspring of the winter sprite
setter's reading: frost nips, so one who nips, and that word is slang for a small child

explanation.walkthrough: Jack Frost bites fingers and noses with cold; one who does so is a nipper, a word that also means a youngster.
explanation.definitionFit: Nipper is informal British slang for a young child, and literally names something that bites with cold.

clue.text: Lodger ran into collision

indicators.note: running into something here means going inside it, between its two letters

parts.note: paying guest, abbreviated PG
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lodger ran into a car crash.
explanation.walkthrough: A prang is British slang for a minor car crash.
explanation.definitionFit: Prang is informal British slang for a crash or bump in a vehicle or aircraft, a collision.

clue.text: Sackable lapses of a Crimean bounder?

indicators.note: lapses are slips, so the letters of the word slip out of their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Fireable slips by a cad stationed in the Crimea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bounder' looks like an old word for a cad; here it means something forming a boundary.
explanation.definitionFit: The Black Sea forms the southern and western coast of the Crimean peninsula, bounding it.

clue.text: Tobacco licensing giving one the gripes

indicators.note: the two words are giving up a run of their letters across the join

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Tobacco licensing rules give someone stomach ache.
explanation.definitionFit: The gripes is an old term for severe abdominal pain, which is what colic is.

clue.text: Interfered with the roofer

definitions.meaning: second meaning: tarred material laid on roofs

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a builder being meddled with; 'the roofer' is not a tradesman but the roofing material.
explanation.definitionFit: To have felt someone is to have touched them improperly, and roofing felt is the bitumen sheet covering a roof.

clue.text: Illegal goal: one, perhaps, that is converted by Italian prodigy

indicators.note: converted means changed into another form, as a rugby try is converted, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
one as a Roman numeral
the abbreviation i.e.

explanation.surface: A disallowed goal is converted by a gifted Italian player, in football or rugby terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Converted' looks like a rugby conversion after a try, but tells you to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Galileo Galilei was the brilliant Italian astronomer and physicist, a genius or prodigy of science.

clue.text: Rural retreat caught by its awful rage

indicators.note: something awful is in a dreadful state, so these letters are in a mess to be sorted

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
c is the cricket abbreviation for caught; it retreats to the back

explanation.surface: A country hideaway is overtaken by somebody's dreadful temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rural retreat' reads as one phrase, but only the first word is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Agrestic is a rare adjective from Latin ager, field, meaning rustic or of the countryside.

clue.text: Clues like this, I see, leave one hollow

indicators.note: letters that leave a word depart from it, so they are taken out

parts.note: the kind of clue you are solving
I, then see said as the letter C

explanation.surface: A solver realises cryptic clues leave them feeling empty.
explanation.walkthrough: CRYPTIC loses its final IC to leave CRYPT.
explanation.definitionFit: A crypt is an underground vault or chamber beneath a church, a hollow space.
